ctci-distinct-badge-code.title: Distinct Badge Code
ctci-distinct-badge-code.description:
A conference prints a short code on every badge. A code is **valid** only when no character appears in it more than once.
Upper-case and lower-case letters count as different characters, and a space is a character like any other.

Write `allDistinct(code)` that returns `True` when every character of `code` is different from all the others, and `False` otherwise.
The empty string is valid.

**Constraints:** `0 <= len(code) <= 10^5`; characters are printable ASCII.

**Example 1:** `code = "kiwi"` → `False` (the letter `i` appears twice)

**Example 2:** `code = "Aa1!"` → `True`

guide.prereqs: Python sets and the idea of a hash table: see [Hash maps and sets](#/lesson/neet-arrays/arrays-hashing-pattern).
guide.intuition: A repeat exists exactly when you meet a character you have already met. A set answers "have I met this before?" in constant time, so one pass is enough.
hints: What would you do by hand? You would keep a list of the characters you have already read.
Which data structure answers "is this in my list?" without scanning the list?
Walk the string once; return False the moment a character is already in your set. If the loop ends, return True.
guide.brute_force: Compare every character with every later character: two nested loops, O(n²) time, O(1) extra space. Fine for 20 characters, hopeless for 100,000.
guide.approach:
Keep an empty set. For each character: if it is in the set, stop with `False`; otherwise add it.

Dry run on `kiwi`: `k` → set {k}; `i` → {k,i}; `w` → {k,i,w}; `i` is already there → `False`.

A useful observation to say aloud: with printable ASCII there are only 95 possible characters, so any string longer than 95 must contain a repeat.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), and in fact O(min(n, alphabet)) because the loop must stop once the alphabet is exhausted. Space O(alphabet) for the set.
guide.pitfalls: Lower-casing the input (the statement says case matters). Comparing only neighbouring characters. Forgetting the empty string.
guide.follow_up: Do it with no extra data structure: sort the characters first (O(n log n)) and compare neighbours, or use one integer as a bit set when the alphabet is a-z. See [Bit tricks](#/lesson/neet-greedy-math/bit-tricks).

ctci-shuffled-twins.title: Shuffled Twins
ctci-shuffled-twins.description:
Two strings are **shuffled twins** when one can be turned into the other only by re-ordering its characters:
nothing is added, removed or changed. Case matters and spaces count.

Write `isShuffle(a, b)` that returns `True` when `a` and `b` are shuffled twins.

**Constraints:** `0 <= len(a), len(b) <= 10^5`.

**Example 1:** `a = "stream", b = "master"` → `True`

**Example 2:** `a = "aab", b = "abb"` → `False` (same letters, different counts)

guide.prereqs: Counting with a dictionary: see [Hash maps and sets](#/lesson/neet-arrays/arrays-hashing-pattern).
guide.intuition: Re-ordering never changes how many times each character occurs. So two strings are twins exactly when their character counts match.
hints: If the lengths differ, can they ever be twins?
Count each character of the first string in a dictionary.
Walk the second string and decrease the counts; a count that would go below zero proves a mismatch.
guide.brute_force: Sort both strings and compare: O(n log n). Shorter to write and perfectly acceptable to mention first.
guide.approach:
1. Different lengths → `False`.
2. Count the characters of `a`.
3. For each character of `b`, take one away; if none is left, return `False`.
4. Lengths were equal, so if nothing went negative every count is now zero.

Dry run `aab` vs `abb`: counts {a:2, b:1}. Read `a` → {a:1,b:1}; `b` → {a:1,b:0}; `b` again → nothing left → `False`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(k) where k is the number of distinct characters.
guide.pitfalls: Comparing sets instead of counts (`aab` and `abb` have the same set). Skipping the length check, which makes the final step wrong.
guide.follow_up: Ask the interviewer whether case and whitespace matter; here they do. The same counting idea solves grouping problems: see [Group Anagrams](#/problem/group-anagrams).

ctci-run-length-shrink.title: Run-Length Shrink
ctci-run-length-shrink.description:
A sensor writes a log made only of letters. To save space we replace every run of the same letter by the letter followed by the run's length:
`"hhhhjjk"` becomes `"h4j2k1"`.

Write `shrink(log)` that returns the shrunk text, **unless** the shrunk text is not strictly shorter than the original, in which case return the original unchanged.

**Constraints:** `0 <= len(log) <= 10^5`; only letters `a-z`, `A-Z` (case matters).

**Example 1:** `"hhhhjjk"` → `"h4j2k1"`

**Example 2:** `"abc"` → `"abc"` (the shrunk form `a1b1c1` is longer)

guide.prereqs: String building and two indexes on one string: see [Two pointers](#/lesson/neet-arrays/two-pointers-pattern).
guide.intuition: A run is a stretch of equal neighbours. Find where each run starts and ends, write letter plus length, then compare lengths once at the end.
hints: Use one index for the start of a run and a second that walks to its end.
Collect the pieces in a list and join once; repeated `+=` on strings copies the text again and again.
Only after building the packed text decide which of the two strings to return.
guide.brute_force: Append to a string with `+=` for every character. In languages with immutable strings this copies the growing string each time and costs O(n²).
guide.approach:
`i` marks a run start. Move `j` forward while `log[j] == log[i]`. Emit `log[i]` and `j - i`, then set `i = j`.

Dry run `hhhhjjk`: run `h` from 0 to 4 → `h4`; run `j` from 4 to 6 → `j2`; run `k` from 6 to 7 → `k1`. Result `h4j2k1` (6 characters) is shorter than 7, so return it.
guide.complexity: Time O(n): each character is visited once by `j`. Space O(n) for the output.
guide.pitfalls: Returning the packed form when it has the *same* length (`aabb` → `a2b2` is not shorter). Counting letters globally instead of per run. Runs of 10 or more need two digits, which `str()` handles.
guide.follow_up: Compute the packed length first without building it, so that you allocate nothing when the answer is the original. Then write a matching `expand` function.

ctci-one-typo-apart.title: One Typo Apart
ctci-one-typo-apart.description:
A spell checker treats two words as *close* when you can turn the first into the second with **at most one** of these typing slips:
insert one character, delete one character, or replace one character by another. Identical words are close (zero slips).

Write `oneTypoApart(a, b)` returning `True` when the words are close.

**Constraints:** `0 <= len(a), len(b) <= 10^5`.

**Example 1:** `a = "plane", b = "plan"` → `True` (delete `e`)

**Example 2:** `a = "plane", b = "blank"` → `False` (two replacements needed)

guide.prereqs: Two pointers moving through two sequences: see [Two pointers](#/lesson/neet-arrays/two-pointers-pattern).
guide.intuition: Insert and delete are the same slip seen from the two sides, so only the length difference matters: equal lengths means "at most one replacement", lengths differing by one means "the longer word has one extra character".
hints: If the lengths differ by two or more, the answer is immediate.
Make `a` the shorter word so that you only handle one direction.
Walk both words. At the first mismatch spend your single allowance: for equal lengths advance both indexes, otherwise advance only the index of the longer word.
guide.brute_force: Generate every string one slip away from `a` and look for `b`: O(n · alphabet) candidates of length n, so O(n²) work or worse.
guide.approach:
Swap so `a` is not longer. If `len(b) - len(a) > 1` return `False`. Scan with `i` on `a`, `j` on `b`. On a mismatch: if a slip was already used, fail; otherwise mark it used and skip one character of `b` (and of `a` too when the lengths are equal).

Dry run `cat` / `coat`: `c=c`; `a≠o` → slip used, lengths differ so only `j` moves; `a=a`; `t=t`; end → `True`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Counting positional mismatches with `zip` fails for inserts (`cat` vs `scat` mismatches at every position). A swap of neighbours (`teh`/`the`) is two replacements, so it is not close.
guide.follow_up: The general version with any number of slips is edit distance: see [Edit Distance](#/problem/edit-distance) and the lesson [DP on strings](#/lesson/neet-dp/dp-strings).

ctci-quarter-turn-grid.title: Quarter-Turn Grid
ctci-quarter-turn-grid.description:
A square photo is stored as an `n × n` grid of integers (one per pixel). Turn the photo **90 degrees clockwise, in place**:
change the grid you are given and return nothing. You may not build a second `n × n` grid.

**Constraints:** `1 <= n <= 200`.

**Example 1:** `[[1,2],[3,4]]` becomes `[[3,1],[4,2]]`

**Example 2:** `[[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]` becomes `[[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]]`

guide.prereqs: 2-D lists and index arithmetic: see [Matrix tricks](#/lesson/neet-greedy-math/matrix-tricks).
guide.intuition: Think of the square as onion rings. In one ring every cell belongs to a group of four cells that trade places: top → right → bottom → left → top. Rotating a ring is a series of four-way swaps.
hints: Where does the cell at row `r`, column `c` end up? At row `c`, column `n-1-r`.
Handle the outer ring first, then the next ring inward. There are `n // 2` rings.
Alternative that is easier to remember: transpose the grid (swap across the main diagonal), then reverse each row.
guide.brute_force: Build a new grid with `new[c][n-1-r] = old[r][c]`. Correct and O(n²) time, but uses O(n²) extra memory, which the statement forbids.
guide.approach:
For each `layer` let `first = layer`, `last = n-1-layer`. For offset `k` from 0 to `last-first-1`, save the top cell, move left → top, bottom → left, right → bottom, saved top → right.

Dry run on the 2×2 example: one layer, `k = 0`. Save top `1`. Top gets left `3`. Left gets bottom `4`. Bottom gets right `2`. Right gets saved `1`. Grid: `[[3,1],[4,2]]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n²) because every cell moves once; that is optimal since every cell must be touched. Space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Looping `k` up to and including `last - first` rotates the corners twice. Transposing only (a mirror, not a turn). Reversing rows and columns gives 180 degrees.
guide.follow_up: Rotate counter-clockwise, or rotate a non-square image (which cannot be done in place in the same way). See [Rotate Image](#/problem/rotate-image) for the transpose-and-reverse view.

ctci-blackout-rows-cols.title: Blackout Rows and Columns
ctci-blackout-rows-cols.description:
A seating chart is an `m × n` grid of integers. A `0` marks a broken seat. For safety, every seat that shares a **row or a column with an originally broken seat** must also be set to `0`.

Change the grid **in place** and return nothing. Zeros that you write yourself must not trigger further blackouts.

**Constraints:** `1 <= m, n <= 200`.

**Example:** `[[4,1,7],[2,0,5],[3,9,6]]` becomes `[[4,0,7],[0,0,0],[3,0,6]]`

guide.prereqs: Nested loops over a grid: see [Matrix tricks](#/lesson/neet-greedy-math/matrix-tricks).
guide.intuition: Separate *finding* from *writing*. First record which rows and columns contain an original zero, then write. The grid's own first row and first column can serve as the notebook, which removes the extra memory.
hints: If you write zeros while scanning, you will later mistake your own zeros for original ones.
A set of row numbers and a set of column numbers is a clean O(m + n) memory solution; present it first.
To reach O(1) memory, store the marks in row 0 and column 0, after remembering in two booleans whether row 0 and column 0 themselves contain a zero.
guide.brute_force: Copy the whole grid, scan the copy and write into the original: O(m·n) extra memory. Or, for each cell, scan its whole row and column: O(m·n·(m+n)) time.
guide.approach:
1. Booleans: does row 0 hold a zero? does column 0?
2. For every other cell that is zero, mark `grid[r][0]` and `grid[0][c]`.
3. For every other cell, zero it when its row mark or column mark is zero.
4. Finally blank row 0 and column 0 if their booleans say so.

Dry run on the example: the zero at (1,1) sets marks `grid[1][0] = 0` and `grid[0][1] = 0`. Step 3 zeroes (1,2) and (2,1). Row 0 and column 0 had no original zero, so only the marks stay zero.
guide.complexity: Time O(m·n), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Cascading: the first wrong solution turns the whole grid to zeros. Using the marker row before saving whether it had a zero of its own. Processing row 0 and column 0 too early destroys the marks.
guide.follow_up: Same problem as [Set Matrix Zeroes](#/problem/set-matrix-zeroes). Discuss what changes if the grid is too large for memory and arrives row by row.

ctci-turned-word.title: Turned Word
ctci-turned-word.description:
Take a word written on a paper ring and cut the ring at some point: you get a **turn** of the word. For example the turns of `"tide"` are `"tide"`, `"idet"`, `"deti"` and `"etid"`.

Write `isTurned(word, other)` that returns `True` when `other` is a turn of `word`.

**Constraints:** `0 <= len(word), len(other) <= 10^5`.

**Example 1:** `word = "lantern", other = "ternlan"` → `True`

**Example 2:** `word = "lantern", other = "ternnal"` → `False`

guide.prereqs: Substring search and string concatenation. See [Pattern matching](#/lesson/dsa-foundations/pattern-matching) for how `in` can be fast.
guide.intuition: Cutting the ring splits the word into a front part `x` and a back part `y`, and the turn is `y + x`. Write the word twice: `x y x y`. The middle of that contains `y x`. So every turn is a substring of the doubled word.
hints: Split the word as `x + y`. What does the turn look like in terms of `x` and `y`?
Where does `y + x` appear inside `x + y + x + y`?
Check equal lengths first, then one substring test on `word + word`.
guide.brute_force: Try all n cut points and compare the n-character result each time: O(n²).
guide.approach:
Return `len(word) == len(other) and other in word + word`.

Dry run: `word + word = lanternlantern`. `ternlan` starts at index 3 → `True`. `ternnal` appears nowhere → `False`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) with a linear-time substring search (O(n) typical for Python's `in`), space O(n) for the doubled string.
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting the length check (`abc` is a substring of `abcabcabcabc` but not a turn of `abcabc`). Comparing sorted letters, which accepts any shuffle.
guide.follow_up: Find the cut position, or decide whether a list is a rotation of another list using [KMP](#/lesson/dsa-foundations/pattern-matching) on the values.

ctci-drop-repeat-nodes.title: Drop Repeat Nodes
ctci-drop-repeat-nodes.description:
A playlist is stored as a singly linked list of track numbers, in no particular order. Remove every node whose value has **already appeared earlier** in the list, keeping the first occurrence and the original order. Return the head.

**Constraints:** `0 <= length <= 10^5`; values fit in 32 bits.

**Example 1:** `4 → 9 → 4 → 2 → 9` → `4 → 9 → 2`

**Example 2:** `7 → 7 → 7` → `7`

guide.prereqs: How a singly linked list is unlinked with a `prev` pointer: see [Linked-list pointers](#/lesson/neet-linked-trees/ll-pointers).
guide.intuition: Removing a node means making the node *before* it point past it. So walk with two references, `prev` and `cur`, and a set of the values met so far.
hints: You need to know whether a value was seen before: which structure gives that in O(1)?
To delete `cur` you must change `prev.next`. Only advance `prev` when you keep the node.
The head is never deleted (it is always a first occurrence), so no dummy node is required here.
guide.brute_force: For each node, run a second pointer through the rest of the list deleting equal values: O(n²) time, O(1) space. This is the answer when the interviewer forbids extra memory.
guide.approach:
Loop while `cur`: if `cur.val` is in `seen`, bypass it with `prev.next = cur.next`; else add the value and move `prev` to `cur`. Always move `cur` forward.

Dry run `4→9→4→2→9`: keep 4, keep 9, third node 4 is seen → 9 now points to 2, keep 2, last 9 is seen → 2 points to nothing. Result `4→9→2`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the set.
guide.pitfalls: Advancing `prev` after a deletion (it would then point at a removed node). Comparing only neighbours, which works only for sorted lists.
guide.follow_up: No-buffer version with the runner technique (O(n²)). For a sorted list see [Remove Duplicates from Sorted List](#/problem/remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list).

ctci-kth-from-tail.title: Kth From the Tail
ctci-kth-from-tail.description:
A relay team is stored as a singly linked list of runner numbers. Return the number worn by the runner who is `k`-th counting **from the end**, where `k = 1` means the last runner. If the list has fewer than `k` nodes, return `-1`.

Do it in **one pass** without first counting the nodes.

**Constraints:** `0 <= length <= 10^5`, `1 <= k <= 10^5`, values are non-negative.

**Example 1:** list `10 → 20 → 30 → 40`, `k = 2` → `30`

**Example 2:** list `10 → 20`, `k = 5` → `-1`

guide.prereqs: Two pointers on one list: see [Fast and slow pointers](#/lesson/neet-linked-trees/ll-fast-slow).
guide.intuition: Two walkers kept exactly `k` nodes apart behave like a ruler: when the front one falls off the end, the back one is `k` nodes from the end.
hints: If you knew the length `n`, the answer is at position `n - k` from the front. How can you avoid counting?
Send one pointer `k` steps ahead. What does it mean if it runs out of nodes during those steps?
Then move both one step at a time until the leader becomes `None`.
guide.brute_force: Count the nodes in a first pass, then walk `n - k` steps in a second pass: O(n) time but two passes. Or copy the values into an array: O(n) space.
guide.approach:
Advance `lead` by `k` nodes, returning `-1` if it is `None` before a step. Then move `lead` and `trail` together until `lead` is `None`.

Dry run `10→20→30→40`, `k=2`: lead goes to 30. Step: lead 40, trail 20. Step: lead None, trail 30. Answer 30.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Off by one: stopping when `lead.next` is `None` returns the (k+1)-th from the end. Not handling `k` larger than the length.
guide.follow_up: Delete that node instead of returning it: see [Remove Nth Node From End of List](#/problem/remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list). A recursive version counts on the way back up the call stack and uses O(n) stack space.

ctci-pivot-split-list.title: Pivot Split
ctci-pivot-split-list.description:
Parcels move on a conveyor belt stored as a singly linked list of weights. Re-arrange the belt so that **every parcel lighter than `pivot` comes before every parcel that weighs `pivot` or more**. Inside each of the two groups the parcels must keep their original relative order. Return the new head.

**Constraints:** `0 <= length <= 10^5`.

**Example:** list `6 → 2 → 9 → 4 → 1`, `pivot = 4` → `2 → 1 → 6 → 9 → 4`

guide.prereqs: Dummy head nodes: see [Linked-list pointers](#/lesson/neet-linked-trees/ll-pointers).
guide.intuition: Build two separate chains while walking once: a "light" chain and a "heavy" chain. Appending at the tail of each chain preserves order. At the end, hook the light tail to the heavy head.
hints: Do not try to shuffle nodes inside one list; grow two lists instead.
A dummy node in front of each chain removes the special case "is this the first node of the chain?".
After the walk, the last heavy node may still point at an old neighbour: set its `next` to `None`.
guide.brute_force: Copy values into two Python lists, concatenate and rebuild the linked list: O(n) time but O(n) extra memory and new nodes.
guide.approach:
Walk `cur`. `val < pivot` → append to `small`; else append to `big`. Then `big.next = None`, `small.next = big_head.next`, return `small_head.next`.

Dry run `6→2→9→4→1`, pivot 4: big: 6; small: 2; big: 6→9; big: 6→9→4; small: 2→1. Join: `2→1→6→9→4`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1): nodes are re-linked, not copied.
guide.pitfalls: Leaving the old `next` of the final heavy node creates a cycle. Sorting changes the order inside the groups. Pushing light nodes at the front reverses them.
guide.follow_up: Three-way version (less than, equal, greater), the linked-list form of the Dutch flag partition used by [Quick sort](#/lesson/dsa-foundations/quick-sort). Compare with [Partition List](#/problem/partition-list).

ctci-digit-list-sum.title: Digit List Sum (Forward Order)
ctci-digit-list-sum.description:
Two non-negative whole numbers are stored as singly linked lists with **one decimal digit per node, most significant digit first**: `3 → 0 → 5` means 305. The lists may have different lengths and there are no leading zeros (except the number 0 itself, stored as a single node `0`).

Return their sum in the same format.

**Constraints:** each list has between 1 and `10^4` nodes. Do not convert the whole list to a Python integer: the point is the digit-by-digit technique.

**Example 1:** `4 → 8 → 3` plus `7 → 5 → 9` → `1 → 2 → 4 → 2` (483 + 759 = 1242)

**Example 2:** `9 → 9` plus `1` → `1 → 0 → 0`

guide.prereqs: Stacks, and adding numbers column by column with a carry: see [Stack basics](#/lesson/neet-window-stack/stack-basics).
guide.intuition: School addition starts at the *last* digit, but a singly linked list only lets you walk forward. A stack reverses the order of arrival, so pushing the digits and popping them gives you the digits from least significant to most significant.
hints: Why can you not add node by node from the heads? Think about `99 + 1`.
Push each list's digits on its own stack, then pop from both.
Create the answer by inserting each new digit in *front* of the result so far; keep going while either stack has digits or the carry is non-zero.
guide.brute_force: Pad the shorter list with leading zero nodes and recurse to the end, returning the carry on the way back: also O(n) but needs O(n) call-stack depth, which fails for 10⁴ nodes in Python's default recursion limit.
guide.approach:
Fill `sa` and `sb`. Loop: `total = carry + pop(sa) + pop(sb)`; new head node holds `total % 10`; `carry = total // 10`.

Dry run 483 + 759: pops 3+9 = 12 → node 2, carry 1; 8+5+1 = 14 → node 4 in front, carry 1; 4+7+1 = 12 → node 2 in front, carry 1; stacks empty but carry 1 → node 1 in front. Result `1→2→4→2`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n + m), space O(n + m) for the stacks.
guide.pitfalls: Adding from the heads treats the lists as if digits were stored in reverse. Dropping the final carry (`99 + 1`).
guide.follow_up: The reverse-order storage is easier and needs no stack: see [Add Two Numbers](#/problem/add-two-numbers). You can also reverse both lists in place, add, and reverse the result for O(1) extra memory.

ctci-mirror-list.title: Mirror List
ctci-mirror-list.description:
A necklace of beads is stored as a singly linked list of colour numbers. Return `True` when the sequence of colours reads the same from the clasp end as from the far end.

Aim for **O(1) extra memory**. An empty list counts as a mirror.

**Constraints:** `0 <= length <= 10^5`.

**Example 1:** `3 → 8 → 8 → 3` → `True`

**Example 2:** `3 → 8 → 5` → `False`

guide.prereqs: Finding the middle with fast and slow pointers and reversing a list: see [Fast and slow pointers](#/lesson/neet-linked-trees/ll-fast-slow) and [Reversal](#/lesson/neet-linked-trees/ll-reversal).
guide.intuition: A mirror sequence equals its own reverse, and you only need to compare the first half with the reversed second half. A list can be reversed by flipping its arrows, with no extra memory.
hints: The easy version copies the values into an array and compares it with its reverse. Say that first.
Find the middle: move one pointer by one node and another by two.
Reverse the part from the middle onward, then walk from both ends toward the centre comparing values.
guide.brute_force: Copy into a Python list and check `vals == vals[::-1]`: O(n) time, O(n) space.
guide.approach:
1. `slow` reaches the middle when `fast` reaches the end.
2. Reverse from `slow` to the end; `prev` is the head of the reversed half.
3. Compare `head...` with `prev...` until the reversed half ends.

Dry run `3→8→8→3`: slow stops at the second 8. Reversed half: `3→8`. Compare 3=3, 8=8 → `True`. With an odd length the middle node sits in the reversed half and is compared with itself, which is harmless.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Comparing only the first and last node. Looping on the *left* half instead of the reversed half walks past the middle. In production code, reverse the second half back before returning so the caller's list is intact.
guide.follow_up: Same task as [Palindrome Linked List](#/problem/palindrome-linked-list). A stack-based variant pushes the first half while the slow pointer walks.

ctci-loop-entry-index.title: Loop Entry Index
ctci-loop-entry-index.description:
A treasure hunt has `n` clue cards numbered `0 … n-1`. Card `i` tells you which card to open next: `nxt[i]`, or `-1` when the hunt ends there. You start at card `0`.

A badly designed hunt can send you round in circles forever. Return the number of the **first card you would visit twice** (the entrance of the loop), or `-1` if the hunt ends normally.

Use **O(1) extra memory**: no set of visited cards and no changes to `nxt`.

**Constraints:** `1 <= n <= 10^5`; each `nxt[i]` is `-1` or in `[0, n-1]`.

**Example 1:** `nxt = [1, 2, 3, 1]` → `1` (path 0, 1, 2, 3, 1, …)

**Example 2:** `nxt = [1, 2, -1]` → `-1`

guide.prereqs: Cycle detection with a slow and a fast pointer: see [Fast and slow pointers](#/lesson/neet-linked-trees/ll-fast-slow).
guide.intuition: The cards form a linked list where `nxt` is the `next` pointer. A walker moving two cards per step must catch a walker moving one card per step if both are trapped in a loop. Where they meet is as far from the loop entrance as the start is (counted modulo the loop length), so a second walk from the start finds the entrance.
hints: First decide only *whether* a loop exists: fast and slow walkers.
The meeting point is usually not the entrance. Draw a list with a tail of 3 cards and a loop of 5 and see where they meet.
After they meet, put one walker back on card 0 and move both one card at a time. They meet at the entrance.
guide.brute_force: Keep a set of visited cards and return the first card already in the set: O(n) time but O(n) memory.
guide.approach:
Let the tail (cards before the loop) have length `t` and the loop length `L`. When slow enters the loop, fast is `t mod L` cards ahead inside it and closes the gap by one per step, so they meet `L - (t mod L)` cards after the entrance. From there, `t` more steps lands exactly on the entrance, and `t` steps from card 0 also lands on the entrance.

Dry run `[1,2,3,1]`: slow 1, fast 2; slow 2, fast 1; slow 3, fast 3 → meet at 3. Reset slow to 0: slow 1, fast 1 → entrance 1.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Returning the meeting point itself. Reading `nxt[-1]`, which in Python silently wraps to the last element: test for `-1` before every jump.
guide.follow_up: The pointer version is LeetCode's *Linked List Cycle II*; the same trick solves [Find the Duplicate Number](#/problem/find-the-duplicate-number).

ctci-floor-stack.title: Floor Stack
ctci-floor-stack.description:
Design a stack of integers that can also report its **smallest element at any moment**, with every operation running in O(1) time.

Implement class `FloorStack`:

- `push(x)` puts `x` on top.
- `pop()` removes the top element and returns it, or returns `-1` if the stack is empty.
- `top()` returns the top element without removing it (`-1` if empty).
- `lowest()` returns the smallest element currently in the stack (`-1` if empty).

**Constraints:** values are in `[0, 10^9]`; up to `10^5` calls.

**Example:** `push(5), push(2), push(8), lowest() → 2, pop() → 8, pop() → 2, lowest() → 5`

guide.prereqs: What a stack is (last in, first out): see [Stack basics](#/lesson/neet-window-stack/stack-basics).
guide.intuition: The minimum can only change when the stack changes, and a stack only changes at the top. So each element can remember "the smallest value at or below me". That note never becomes wrong while the element is in the stack, because nothing below it can change.
hints: A single variable holding the minimum breaks on `pop`: after removing the minimum, what is the new one?
Store extra information next to each pushed value.
Push the pair (value, minimum so far). `lowest()` reads the pair on top.
guide.brute_force: Scan the whole stack in `lowest()`: correct but O(n) per call.
guide.approach:
`push(x)`: floor = `min(x, floor of current top)`; append `(x, floor)`. `pop`/`top` use the first field, `lowest` the second.

Dry run: push 5 → (5,5); push 2 → (2,2); push 8 → (8,2); lowest 2; pop 8; pop 2; top pair is (5,5) so lowest 5.
guide.complexity: Every operation O(1) time. Space O(n): one extra number per element.
guide.pitfalls: Tracking the minimum in one variable (shown in the wrong solution). With a separate min-stack, pushing only on *strictly* smaller values loses duplicates of the minimum; use `<=`.
guide.follow_up: Save memory with a second stack that stores a new minimum only when it changes. Compare with [Min Stack](#/problem/min-stack). Then design a queue with a `highest()` operation using a monotonic deque: see [Monotonic deque](#/lesson/neet-window-stack/monotonic-deque).

ctci-relay-queue.title: Relay Queue From Two Stacks
ctci-relay-queue.description:
You are given only stacks (Python lists used with `append` and `pop()` at the end). Build a first-in, first-out queue from **two stacks**.

Implement class `RelayQueue`:

- `enqueue(x)` adds `x` at the back.
- `dequeue()` removes and returns the front element, or `-1` if the queue is empty.
- `front()` returns the front element without removing it (`-1` if empty).
- `size()` returns the number of stored elements.

Each operation must cost O(1) **amortised** time (averaged over any long sequence of calls).

**Example:** `enqueue(4), enqueue(6), front() → 4, dequeue() → 4, enqueue(9), dequeue() → 6, dequeue() → 9, dequeue() → -1`

guide.prereqs: Stacks, queues and amortised cost: see [Queues and deques](#/lesson/dsa-foundations/queues-deques) and [Dynamic arrays](#/lesson/dsa-foundations/dynamic-arrays).
guide.intuition: Pouring a stack into another stack reverses its order. Reversed last-in-first-out is first-in-first-out. So keep an *inbox* stack for arrivals and an *outbox* stack for departures, and pour only when the outbox is empty.
hints: Pop everything from one stack onto another and look at the order.
If you pour on every dequeue you do far too much work, and pouring while the outbox still holds items puts newer elements in front of older ones.
Pour **only when the outbox is empty**. Then each element is pushed twice and popped twice in its whole life.
guide.brute_force: Keep one stack; on each dequeue pour everything into a temporary stack, take the bottom item, pour everything back: O(n) per dequeue.
guide.approach:
`enqueue` appends to `inbox`. `dequeue`/`front` first call `_shift`, which moves all of `inbox` to `outbox` only if `outbox` is empty.

Dry run: enqueue 4, 6 → inbox [4,6]. front: shift → outbox [6,4], top is 4. dequeue → 4. enqueue 9 → inbox [9]. dequeue → outbox still has 6. dequeue → outbox empty, shift → [9] → 9.
guide.complexity: Amortised O(1) per operation: an element moves inbox → outbox once. A single dequeue can cost O(n). Space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Pouring when the outbox is not empty breaks the order (the wrong solution returns 2 after 3 in the fourth test). Forgetting that `front` also needs the shift.
guide.follow_up: Same idea as [Implement Queue using Stacks](#/problem/implement-queue-using-stacks). Try the mirror image: a stack from two queues, and explain why that one cannot be amortised O(1) for both push and pop with the simple approach.

ctci-book-piles.title: Book Piles
ctci-book-piles.description:
A second-hand bookshop keeps returned books in piles along its counter. A pile is steady only up to `cap` books, so when the newest pile is full, the next book starts a fresh pile to its right. Books are identified by integer codes.

Implement class `BookPiles(cap)`:

- `push(x)` lays book `x` on the rightmost pile (starting a new pile if there is none or the rightmost one is full).
- `pop()` removes and returns the top book of the **rightmost** pile, or `-1` when the counter is empty.
- `popAt(i)` removes and returns the top book of pile number `i` (0 = leftmost), or `-1` if that pile does not exist. Books are **not** moved between piles afterwards, so a pile in the middle may stay shorter than `cap`.
- `count()` returns the current number of piles.

A pile that loses its last book disappears at once and the piles to its right are renumbered one position to the left.

**Constraints:** `1 <= cap <= 100`; up to `2·10^4` calls.

**Example (cap = 2):** `push 1, 2, 3, 4, 5` gives piles `[1,2] [3,4] [5]`. `popAt(0) → 2`, `pop() → 5`, `count() → 2`, `pop() → 4`.

guide.prereqs: A list of lists, and stack operations on each inner list: see [Stacks](#/lesson/dsa-foundations/stacks).
guide.intuition: The structure is a stack of stacks. All the difficulty is in the rules at the boundaries: when to open a new pile and what happens to an empty one. Write those rules down before coding.
hints: Represent the row of piles as a list of lists.
`pop()` is `popAt(last index)`: write one of them in terms of the other.
After removing a book, delete the pile if it is now empty so that no empty pile is ever stored.
guide.brute_force: One flat list plus arithmetic on indexes works for `push`/`pop` but `popAt` leaves holes that the arithmetic cannot describe.
guide.approach:
`push`: if there is no pile or the last is full, append a new empty pile; append the book to the last pile. `popAt(i)`: validate `i`, pop from pile `i`, delete the pile if empty.

Dry run (cap 2): piles `[1,2] [3,4] [5]`. `popAt(0)` → 2, piles `[1] [3,4] [5]`. `pop()` → 5 and the third pile vanishes. `count()` → 2. `pop()` → 4.
guide.complexity: `push`, `pop`, `count`: O(1). `popAt`: O(1) for the pop plus O(t) when a middle pile is deleted from a list of `t` piles.
guide.pitfalls: Leaving empty piles in the list, so that a later `pop` hits an empty list or `count` is too large. Accepting negative indexes, which Python happily interprets as counting from the end.
guide.follow_up: Discuss the alternative rule where `popAt` *does* shift books left so every pile except the last stays full: each `popAt` then costs O(number of piles) and needs a remove-from-bottom operation, which suggests deques.

ctci-sort-with-spare-stack.title: Sort With One Spare Stack
ctci-sort-with-spare-stack.description:
A stack of numbered crates is given as a list whose **last element is the top**. Re-order it so that the **smallest crate is on top** (so the list ends up in descending order from bottom to top) and return it.

The exercise: use only **one additional stack** and a handful of variables. Treat both lists strictly as stacks (`append`, `pop()`, look at `[-1]`, test for empty). Calling `sort` defeats the purpose.

**Constraints:** `0 <= len(stack) <= 2000`.

**Example:** `[3, 1, 4, 1, 5]` → `[5, 4, 3, 1, 1]`

guide.prereqs: Stack operations and insertion sort: see [Stacks](#/lesson/dsa-foundations/stacks).
guide.intuition: Keep the spare stack sorted at all times (largest on top). To add a new crate, temporarily move the crates that are larger than it back onto the original stack, drop the new crate in, and the moved crates will be re-inserted by the same loop later. This is insertion sort, with the original stack doubling as the temporary storage.
hints: Suppose the spare stack is already sorted. How do you insert one more value at the right depth?
Hold the new crate in a variable; pop larger crates from the spare back onto the input stack.
At the end the spare has the largest on top; pour it back once so the smallest ends on top.
guide.brute_force: Repeatedly scan the stack for its minimum by pouring into the spare and back: also O(n²) but with more moving. Using three stacks allows merge sort in O(n log n).
guide.approach:
Loop while the input is non-empty: `crate = stack.pop()`; while the spare's top is greater than `crate`, move it back to the input; push `crate` on the spare. Finally pour the spare into the input.

Dry run `[3,1,4]` (top 4): spare [4]. crate 1: 4 > 1 → move 4 back, spare [1], input [3,4]. crate 4 → spare [1,4]. crate 3: 4 > 3 → back, spare [1,3], input [4]. crate 4 → spare [1,3,4]. Pour: `[4,3,1]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n²) in the worst case (input already in the wrong order), space O(n) for the spare stack.
guide.pitfalls: Using `if` instead of `while` moves back only one crate, leaving the spare unsorted. Returning ascending order: read which end is the top.
guide.follow_up: How would you sort if you had unlimited stacks? Split and merge (merge sort), or partition around a pivot (quick sort): see [Merge sort](#/lesson/dsa-foundations/merge-sort).

ctci-triple-stack-array.title: Three Stacks, One Array
ctci-triple-stack-array.description:
Memory is tight on a microcontroller: you get **one fixed array** and must run three independent stacks inside it. Each stack gets an equal slice of `cap` slots.

Implement class `TripleStack(cap)` where `s` is the stack number `0`, `1` or `2`:

- `push(s, x)` pushes `x` on stack `s`; returns `True`, or `False` (and stores nothing) if that stack already holds `cap` values.
- `pop(s)` removes and returns the top of stack `s`, or `-1` if it is empty.
- `peek(s)` returns the top of stack `s` without removing it, or `-1`.
- `sizes()` returns a list with the three current sizes.

Store all values in a single list of length `3 * cap`; do not create three lists.

**Constraints:** `1 <= cap <= 1000`; values in `[0, 10^9]`.

**Example (cap = 2):** `push(0,5) → True, push(0,6) → True, push(0,7) → False, push(2,9) → True, pop(0) → 6, peek(2) → 9, pop(1) → -1, sizes() → [1,0,1]`

guide.prereqs: Array indexing and how an array-backed stack keeps a size counter: see [Stacks](#/lesson/dsa-foundations/stacks).
guide.intuition: Cut the array into three equal regions. Stack `s` owns slots `s*cap … s*cap + cap - 1`. A stack needs only one number of bookkeeping, its size, because the top is always at `start + size - 1`.
hints: Where does region `s` begin? At index `s * cap`.
Keep a list of three sizes. The next free slot of stack `s` is `s * cap + size[s]`.
`pop` only has to decrease the size and read the slot: the old value can stay in the array as garbage.
guide.brute_force: Three separate Python lists: trivial but ignores the single-array requirement, which is the point of the exercise.
guide.approach:
`push(s, x)`: full if `used[s] == cap`; else write at `s*cap + used[s]` and increment. `pop(s)`: empty if `used[s] == 0`; else decrement and read.

Dry run (cap 2): push(0,5) writes index 0; push(0,6) writes index 1; push(0,7) refused; push(2,9) writes index 4; pop(0) reads index 1 → 6.
guide.complexity: All operations O(1) time; space is the fixed `3 * cap` array plus three counters.
guide.pitfalls: Checking total capacity instead of the per-stack capacity lets stack 0 overflow into stack 1's region. Reading before decrementing in `pop` returns the slot above the top.
guide.follow_up: The harder design lets the regions have flexible sizes: when one stack is full but the array is not, shift a neighbouring region and treat the array as circular. Discuss the cost of shifting and why it is rarely worth it.

ctci-repair-counter.title: Repair Counter
ctci-repair-counter.description:
A repair shop fixes two kinds of device, phones and laptops, strictly in the order in which they were handed in. A technician who becomes free asks either for "whichever device has waited longest" or, depending on their training, for the longest-waiting phone or the longest-waiting laptop.

Implement class `RepairCounter`:

- `dropOff(tag, kind)` registers a device; `tag` is the label stuck on it and `kind` is `"phone"` or `"laptop"`.
- `takeAny()` removes and returns the tag of the device that was handed in earliest.
- `takePhone()` / `takeLaptop()` remove and return the tag of the earliest device of that kind.

Each take method returns the empty string `""` when no suitable device is waiting. All operations must be O(1).

**Example:** `dropOff("P17","phone"), dropOff("L04","laptop"), dropOff("P18","phone"), takeLaptop() → "L04", takeAny() → "P17", takeAny() → "P18", takePhone() → ""`

guide.prereqs: Queues and `collections.deque`: see [Queues and deques](#/lesson/dsa-foundations/queues-deques).
guide.intuition: One queue makes `takePhone` slow (you must dig past laptops). Two queues, one per kind, make the specific requests easy, and a ticket number stamped at drop-off tells you which of the two front devices has waited longer.
hints: What goes wrong with a single queue when someone asks for a laptop and ten phones are in front?
Keep a queue of phones and a queue of laptops. How will you compare the two fronts?
Give every drop-off an increasing ticket number and store it with the tag.
guide.brute_force: A single list, scanning from the front for the first device of the requested kind and deleting it: O(n) per request.
guide.approach:
`dropOff` appends `(ticket, tag)` to the right deque and increments the ticket. `takeAny` compares the tickets at the two fronts (handling an empty deque first) and delegates to `takePhone` or `takeLaptop`.

Dry run: P17(0,phone), L04(1,laptop), P18(2,phone). takeLaptop → L04. takeAny: only phones left → P17. takeAny → P18. takePhone → "".
guide.complexity: O(1) time per operation, O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls: Preferring phones whenever a phone is waiting (wrong solution) ignores the hand-in order. Using tags as the ordering key: tags are not ordered by time.
guide.follow_up: Extend to k kinds of device: `takeAny` then needs the minimum over k queue fronts, which is a job for a heap. See [Binary heaps](#/lesson/neet-heap-graphs/binary-heaps).

ctci-route-exists.title: Route Exists
ctci-route-exists.description:
A city has `n` crossings numbered `0 … n-1` joined by **one-way** streets. `streets[i] = [a, b]` means you can drive from `a` to `b` (not back).

Return `True` if a car can get from crossing `src` to crossing `dst` by following streets, `False` otherwise. A crossing can always reach itself.

**Constraints:** `1 <= n <= 10^4`; `0 <= len(streets) <= 2·10^4`.

**Example 1:** `n = 4, streets = [[0,1],[1,2],[3,2]], src = 0, dst = 2` → `True`

**Example 2:** same streets, `src = 2, dst = 0` → `False`

guide.prereqs: Adjacency lists and breadth-first search: see [Graph representations](#/lesson/neet-heap-graphs/graph-representations) and [DFS and BFS](#/lesson/neet-heap-graphs/dfs-bfs).
guide.intuition: "Can I get there?" is plain graph search. Start at `src`, repeatedly visit everything one street away from places you already reached, and never visit a crossing twice.
hints: Turn the list of streets into, for each crossing, the list of crossings you can drive to.
Use a queue (breadth-first) or a stack (depth-first); either works for a yes/no answer.
Mark a crossing as seen when you put it in the queue, not when you take it out, so that it is never queued twice.
guide.brute_force: Repeat n times: scan all streets and mark `b` reachable whenever `a` is. That is O(n·m), the idea behind Bellman-Ford.
guide.approach:
Build `out[a]`. BFS from `src` with a `seen` array. Return `True` when `dst` is dequeued; `False` when the queue empties.

Dry run example 1: queue [0] → visit 0, add 1 → visit 1, add 2 → visit 2 = dst → `True`. Example 2 starts at 2, which has no outgoing street → `False`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n + m), space O(n + m).
guide.pitfalls: Treating streets as two-way. Forgetting the `seen` marks, which loops forever on a cycle. Recursion-based DFS can exceed Python's recursion limit on a long chain; an explicit stack or queue avoids that.
guide.follow_up: Find the shortest route (BFS gives it for free by recording distances), or search from both ends at once: see the problem [Friend Hops](#/problem/ctci-friend-hops).

ctci-balanced-bst-from-sorted.title: Balanced Tree From Sorted Scores
ctci-balanced-bst-from-sorted.description:
You receive exam scores **sorted in increasing order with no repeats**. Build a binary search tree of the smallest possible height that contains them and return its root.

So that everybody produces the same tree, always choose the element at index `(lo + hi) // 2` of the current range `lo … hi` as the root of that range.

**Constraints:** `0 <= len(scores) <= 10^4`.

**Example:** `[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]` → root 30; left subtree built from `[10, 20]` (root 10, right child 20); right subtree from `[40, 50]` (root 40, right child 50). Level order: `[30, 10, 40, null, 20, null, 50]`.

guide.prereqs: Binary search trees and recursion on index ranges: see [BST lesson](#/lesson/neet-linked-trees/tree-bst).
guide.intuition: A tree is shortest when each node splits its values as evenly as possible. In a sorted array, the middle element splits the rest into two equal halves that are themselves sorted, so the same idea applies to each half.
hints: Which element should be the root so that the two sides have (almost) the same number of nodes?
Everything left of the middle is smaller, everything right is larger: exactly the BST rule.
Recurse on index ranges `(lo, mid-1)` and `(mid+1, hi)`; never slice the list.
guide.brute_force: Insert the scores one by one with the ordinary BST insert. Inserting sorted data produces a chain of height n, the worst possible tree, and costs O(n²).
guide.approach:
`build(lo, hi)`: empty range → `None`; else `mid = (lo+hi)//2`, node = `scores[mid]`, children from the two sub-ranges.

Dry run `[10,20,30,40,50]`: mid 2 → 30. Left range (0,1): mid 0 → 10, its right child from (1,1) → 20. Right range (3,4): mid 3 → 40 with right child 50.
guide.complexity: Time O(n): one node per element, O(1) work each. Space O(n) for the tree plus O(log n) recursion depth.
guide.pitfalls: Slicing (`scores[:mid]`) copies data and makes the build O(n log n). Using the upper middle changes the shape; both are balanced but the checker here expects the lower middle.
guide.follow_up: Same as [Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree](#/problem/convert-sorted-array-to-binary-search-tree). Harder: build from a sorted *linked list* in O(n) by constructing in in-order.

ctci-level-headed-tree.title: Level-Headed Tree
ctci-level-headed-tree.description:
Call a binary tree **level-headed** when, at *every* node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most one. (The height of an empty subtree is 0.)

Return `True` if the given tree is level-headed. Aim for a single traversal.

**Constraints:** up to `10^4` nodes; the tree's height is at most 500.

**Example 1:** `[1, 2, 3, 4]` → `True`

**Example 2:** `[1, 2, null, 3]` (a chain of three going left) → `False`

guide.prereqs: Tree height and post-order recursion: see [Returning values up the tree](#/lesson/neet-linked-trees/tree-return-up).
guide.intuition: Each node needs two facts about each child: its height, and whether it is already unbalanced. One recursive function can return both if you reserve a special value (−1) for "unbalanced below".
hints: Checking only the root's two children is not enough: the imbalance may be deep inside one side.
Computing a fresh height at every node repeats work. Can the height function report a problem as well?
Return −1 as soon as a subtree is unbalanced and pass that −1 straight up.
guide.brute_force: For every node call a separate `height` function on both children, then recurse into the children: O(n log n) on balanced trees and O(n²) on a chain.
guide.approach:
`height(node)`: empty → 0. Get left; if −1 return −1. Get right; if −1 or the difference exceeds 1 return −1. Else `1 + max`.

Dry run `[1,2,null,3]`: node 3 → 1; node 2 → left 1, right 0 → 2; node 1 → left 2, right 0, difference 2 → −1 → `False`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) for the recursion where h is the height.
guide.pitfalls: Testing only the root (the ninth test is balanced at the root but not below). Mixing up height in nodes versus edges is harmless here as long as you are consistent.
guide.follow_up: Same check as [Balanced Binary Tree](#/problem/balanced-binary-tree). Balanced search trees maintain this property automatically: see [AVL trees](#/lesson/dsa-foundations/avl).

ctci-valid-search-tree.title: Valid Search Tree
ctci-valid-search-tree.description:
A library index is supposed to be a **binary search tree**: for every node, *all* values in its left subtree are strictly smaller and *all* values in its right subtree are strictly larger. Duplicates are therefore not allowed.

Return `True` if the given binary tree satisfies the rule.

**Constraints:** up to `10^4` nodes; height at most 500; values fit in 32-bit signed integers.

**Example 1:** `[8, 3, 10, 1, 6]` → `True`

**Example 2:** `[8, 3, 10, 1, 9]` → `False` (9 sits in the left subtree of 8)

guide.prereqs: The BST property and in-order traversal: see [BST lesson](#/lesson/neet-linked-trees/tree-bst).
guide.intuition: The rule talks about whole subtrees, not only a node's two children. Carry a permitted range down the tree: going left tightens the upper limit to the parent's value, going right tightens the lower limit.
hints: Comparing each node only with its children accepts example 2. Why?
What range of values is allowed for the right child of the root's left child?
Pass `(low, high)` down; use `None` for "no limit" rather than a magic number.
guide.brute_force: For every node, compute the maximum of its left subtree and the minimum of its right subtree: O(n²) on a chain.
guide.approach:
`ok(node, low, high)`: empty → True; value outside the open interval → False; recurse left with `(low, val)` and right with `(val, high)`.

Dry run example 2: 8 with (None, None) fine; 3 with (None, 8) fine; 9 as right child of 3 has range (3, 8): 9 ≥ 8 → `False`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(h).
guide.pitfalls: Local parent-child comparison only. Using `<=`/`>=` the wrong way round and accepting duplicates. Using ±2³¹ as sentinels breaks when the tree contains those very values.
guide.follow_up: Alternative: an in-order traversal of a BST must be strictly increasing; keep only the previous value. See [Validate Binary Search Tree](#/problem/validate-binary-search-tree).

ctci-inorder-next-value.title: Next Larger Entry
ctci-inorder-next-value.description:
A binary search tree stores distinct appointment times (integers). Given a number `t` (which may or may not be in the tree), return the **smallest stored value that is strictly greater than `t`**, or `-1` if no such value exists.

Do not visit the whole tree: the running time should depend on the tree's height.

**Constraints:** up to `10^4` nodes; values and `t` are in `[0, 10^9]`.

**Example:** tree `[20, 10, 30, 5, 15]`: `t = 10` → `15`; `t = 16` → `20`; `t = 30` → `-1`

guide.prereqs: Searching in a BST: see [BST lesson](#/lesson/neet-linked-trees/tree-bst).
guide.intuition: Walk down as if searching for `t`. Every time you turn left you pass a node that is larger than `t`: it is a candidate, and each later candidate is smaller than the previous one. The last candidate you saw is the answer.
hints: At a node with value > t, the answer is this node or something smaller on its left.
At a node with value ≤ t, nothing on its left can be the answer.
Keep one variable `best`; update it on every left turn.
guide.brute_force: In-order traversal into a sorted list, then binary search: O(n) time and memory.
guide.approach:
Loop from the root: if `node.val > t`, record it and go left; else go right. Return the record.

Dry run `t = 16` on `[20,10,30,5,15]`: 20 > 16 → best 20, go left; 10 ≤ 16 → right; 15 ≤ 16 → right (empty). Answer 20.
guide.complexity: Time O(h), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: The textbook rule "leftmost node of the right subtree" covers only half the cases: when the node has no right child the successor is an ancestor (the wrong solution returns −1 for `t = 15`). It also fails when `t` is not in the tree.
guide.follow_up: With parent pointers you can start from the node itself and climb until you arrive from a left child. Related: [Kth Smallest Element in a BST](#/problem/kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst).

ctci-compile-order.title: Compile Order
ctci-compile-order.description:
A software product has `n` modules numbered `0 … n-1`. `needs[i] = [a, b]` means module `a` **must be compiled before** module `b`.

Return any order of all `n` modules that respects every requirement. If the requirements contradict each other (a circular dependency), return an empty list.

**Constraints:** `1 <= n <= 10^4`; `0 <= len(needs) <= 2·10^4`. Any valid order is accepted.

**Example 1:** `n = 4, needs = [[0,1],[0,2],[1,3],[2,3]]` → `[0,1,2,3]` or `[0,2,1,3]`

**Example 2:** `n = 2, needs = [[0,1],[1,0]]` → `[]`

guide.prereqs: Directed graphs and topological sorting: see [Cycles and topological sort](#/lesson/neet-heap-graphs/cycles-toposort).
guide.intuition: A module can be compiled once everything it waits for is done. Start with the modules that wait for nothing; finishing a module may free others. If you run out of free modules before all are compiled, the remaining ones wait for each other in a circle.
hints: For each module count how many requirements point *into* it (its in-degree).
Put every module with count 0 in a queue. Removing a module lowers the counts of the modules that depend on it.
At the end compare the length of your order with `n` to detect a cycle.
guide.brute_force: Repeatedly scan all modules looking for one whose prerequisites are all done: O(n · (n + m)).
guide.approach:
This is Kahn's algorithm. Build `after[a]` lists and `waiting[b]` counts. Pop from the ready queue, append to the order, decrement the dependants.

Dry run example 1: waiting = [0,1,1,2]; ready [0]. Take 0 → waiting [_,0,0,2], ready [1,2]. Take 1 → 3 waits 1. Take 2 → 3 ready. Take 3. Order `[0,1,2,3]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n + m), space O(n + m).
guide.pitfalls: Returning a partial order when there is a cycle. A repeated requirement must be counted twice in `waiting` (and is decremented twice), which the simple algorithm does naturally. A self-dependency `[0,0]` is a cycle.
guide.follow_up: A depth-first version adds a node after all nodes reachable from it and reverses at the end. Compare with [Course Schedule II](#/problem/course-schedule-ii). The review lesson [Useful maths and graph algorithms](#/lesson/interview-prep/review-math-graphs) revisits both versions.

ctci-shared-ancestor.title: Shared Ancestor
ctci-shared-ancestor.description:
A company's reporting chart is a binary tree in which every node holds a distinct employee number. Given two employee numbers `p` and `q`, return the number of their **lowest shared manager**: the deepest node that has both of them in its subtree (a node counts as being in its own subtree).

The tree is **not** a search tree and nodes have no parent links. If either number does not appear in the tree, return `-1`.

**Constraints:** up to `10^4` nodes; height at most 500; `p != q`.

**Example:** tree `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, 6]`: `p = 4, q = 5` → `2`; `p = 4, q = 6` → `1`; `p = 2, q = 4` → `2`; `p = 4, q = 99` → `-1`

guide.prereqs: Post-order traversal that returns information to the parent: see [Returning values up the tree](#/lesson/neet-linked-trees/tree-return-up).
guide.intuition: Ask every subtree one question: "how many of the two targets do you contain?" The first node (deepest, because children report before parents) whose count reaches 2 is the lowest shared manager.
hints: Each call should return 0, 1 or 2.
A node's count is its children's counts plus one if the node itself is a target.
Record the answer the first time a count equals 2; post-order guarantees that this is the deepest such node.
guide.brute_force: Find the root-to-node path for `p` and for `q` (two traversals, O(n) memory each) and compare the paths from the top until they diverge.
guide.approach:
`count(node)` returns the number of targets below. When it first equals 2, store `node.val`.

Dry run `p=4, q=5`: node 4 → 1, node 5 → 1, node 2 → 0+1+1 = 2 → answer 2. Node 1 later also counts 2 but the answer is already set.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(h).
guide.pitfalls: The classic short solution (shown as the wrong answer) stops descending when it meets `p`, so it never learns whether `q` exists at all: it returns 4 for `p = 4, q = 99`. Always ask whether both nodes are guaranteed to be present.
guide.follow_up: With parent links the problem becomes "intersection of two linked lists". For a BST use the values to steer: see [Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree](#/problem/lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-search-tree).

ctci-downward-path-count.title: Downward Paths With a Given Total
ctci-downward-path-count.description:
Each node of a binary tree holds an integer (possibly negative). Count the paths whose values add up to exactly `target`.

A path may start at **any node** and end at **any node below it (or at itself)**, always moving from parent to child.

**Constraints:** up to `6000` nodes; height at most 500; values in `[-1000, 1000]`.

**Example:** tree `[4, 3, -1, 1, 2]` (4 has children 3 and −1; 3 has children 1 and 2). With `target = 7` → `1` (the path 4 → 3). With `target = 3` → `2` (the single node 3, and the path 4 → −1).

guide.prereqs: Prefix sums with a hash map, and depth-first search: see [Prefix sums and counting](#/lesson/neet-arrays/prefix-counting).
guide.intuition: Along one root-to-node route, the tree is an array. In an array, a stretch sums to `target` exactly when two running totals differ by `target`. So carry the running total down the tree and keep a dictionary of how many times each earlier total occurred on the *current* route.
hints: Solve the array version first: count subarrays with a given sum.
At a node with running total `r`, the number of paths ending here is the number of ancestors (or the empty start) whose running total was `r - target`.
When you leave a node, remove its running total from the dictionary: it must not be visible from other branches.
guide.brute_force: From every node start a fresh downward search that counts paths beginning there: O(n·h), which is O(n²) for a chain.
guide.approach:
`seen = {0: 1}`. At each node: `running += val`; add `seen[running - target]`; increment `seen[running]`; recurse; decrement.

Dry run tree `[4,3,-1,1,2]`, target 3: at 4 running 4, need 1 → 0. At 3 running 7, need 4 → 1 (the path `3`). At 1 running 8, need 5 → 0. At 2 running 9, need 6 → 0. At −1 running 3, need 0 → 1 (path 4 → −1). Total 2.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) for the dictionary and the recursion.
guide.pitfalls: Counting only paths that start at the root (wrong solution). Forgetting to undo the dictionary entry on the way back, which counts "paths" that jump between branches. Not seeding `seen[0] = 1`.
guide.follow_up: Same technique as LeetCode's *Path Sum III* and [Subarray Sum Equals K](#/problem/subarray-sum-equals-k).

ctci-bst-arrival-orders.title: Arrival Orders That Build the Same Tree
ctci-bst-arrival-orders.description:
A binary search tree was built by inserting distinct numbers one at a time into an empty tree, with no rebalancing. Many different insertion orders can lead to the same final tree: for the tree with root 2 and children 1 and 3, both `2,1,3` and `2,3,1` work.

Given the final tree, return **how many insertion orders produce exactly this tree**, modulo `1_000_000_007`. The empty tree has exactly one order (the empty one).

**Constraints:** up to `5000` nodes; height at most 500. The input is guaranteed to be a valid search tree.

**Example 1:** `[2, 1, 3]` → `2`

**Example 2:** `[5, 3, 8, 2, 4]` → `8`

guide.prereqs: BST insertion, and counting with binomial coefficients $\binom{n}{k}$: see [BST lesson](#/lesson/neet-linked-trees/tree-bst) and [Useful maths](#/lesson/interview-prep/review-math-graphs).
guide.intuition: The root must arrive first. After that, the left-subtree values and the right-subtree values never interact: each group must keep an order that builds its own subtree, but the two groups may be interleaved in any way. Counting interleavings of a sequence of length `a` with one of length `b` is choosing which `a` of the `a+b` positions belong to the first: $\binom{a+b}{a}$.
hints: Which value is forced to be first in every valid order?
If the left subtree has `a` nodes and `W_L` valid orders, and the right has `b` and `W_R`, how many ways can one left order and one right order be merged while keeping each one's internal order?
ways(node) = C(a+b, a) × ways(left) × ways(right). Compute sizes and ways bottom-up; precompute factorials modulo the prime.
guide.brute_force: Generate all n! permutations, build a tree from each and compare: impossible beyond about 10 nodes.
guide.approach:
List nodes so that parents come before children, then process the list backwards so children are done first. Keep `size` and `ways` per node.

Dry run `[5,3,8,2,4]`: leaves 2, 4, 8 → size 1, ways 1. Node 3: a = b = 1 → C(2,1) = 2 → ways 2. Root: a = 3, b = 1 → C(4,3) = 4 → 4 × 2 × 1 = 8.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) after O(n) factorials (plus O(n log MOD) for the modular inverses), space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Multiplying by 2 for each node with two children undercounts (it gives 4 for example 2). Forgetting the modulus on intermediate products. Recursing on a tall tree without care for the recursion limit: the reference uses an explicit stack.
guide.follow_up: Print the actual orders for a small tree by "weaving" two lists recursively. Related counting: LeetCode's *Unique Binary Search Trees*.

ctci-splice-bits.title: Splice Bits
ctci-splice-bits.description:
A device register is a 32-bit unsigned number `reg`. You must overwrite the bit positions `lo … hi` (inclusive, position 0 is the least significant bit) with the value `field`, leaving all other bits untouched. `field` is guaranteed to fit in `hi - lo + 1` bits.

Return the new register value.

**Constraints:** `0 <= lo <= hi <= 31`; `0 <= reg < 2^32`.

**Example:** `reg = 0b11111111` (255), `field = 0b010` (2), `lo = 3, hi = 5` → `0b11010111` (215)

guide.prereqs: Binary numbers and the operators `&`, `|`, `~`, `<<`: see [Bits in Python](#/lesson/neet-greedy-math/bits-python).
guide.intuition: Writing a field is two steps: first make a hole (force the target bits to 0), then drop the new bits into the hole with OR. A hole is made by AND-ing with a mask that has 0s exactly where the hole should be.
hints: OR alone can turn 0s into 1s but can never turn a 1 into a 0.
Build a block of `width` ones with `(1 << width) - 1`, then shift it to position `lo`.
Clear with `reg & ~mask`, then OR in `field << lo`.
guide.brute_force: Loop over the positions `lo … hi`, clearing or setting one bit at a time with single-bit masks: correct, O(width), more code.
guide.approach:
`width = hi - lo + 1`; `mask = ((1 << width) - 1) << lo`; answer `(reg & ~mask) | (field << lo)`.

Dry run: width 3, mask `0b00111000`. `reg & ~mask` = `0b11000111`. `field << 3` = `0b00010000`. OR → `0b11010111` = 215.
guide.complexity: O(1) time and space.
guide.pitfalls: Skipping the clearing step. An off-by-one width (`hi - lo`) leaves the top bit of the field's range dirty. In Python `~mask` is negative; AND-ing with `0xFFFFFFFF` keeps the result in 32 bits.
guide.follow_up: Write `extract(reg, lo, hi)` that reads a field back. These two helpers are how network headers and file formats are packed: see [Bit tricks](#/lesson/neet-greedy-math/bit-tricks).

ctci-bit-flips-between.title: Bit Flips Between Two Numbers
ctci-bit-flips-between.description:
Two machines hold the non-negative integers `a` and `b`. How many individual bits of `a` would you have to flip (0 → 1 or 1 → 0) to make it equal to `b`?

**Constraints:** `0 <= a, b < 2^62`. Do not convert the numbers to strings.

**Example 1:** `a = 44 (101100), b = 37 (100101)` → `2`

**Example 2:** `a = 8, b = 8` → `0`

guide.prereqs: XOR and counting set bits: see [Bit tricks](#/lesson/neet-greedy-math/bit-tricks).
guide.intuition: XOR writes a 1 exactly in the positions where two numbers disagree. So the question becomes: how many 1 bits does `a ^ b` have?
hints: Which operator gives 1 when two bits differ and 0 when they agree?
Now count the 1 bits of that result.
`x & (x - 1)` removes the lowest 1 bit of `x`; repeat until `x` is 0 and count the repetitions.
guide.brute_force: Compare the two numbers bit by bit for 62 positions with shifts: fine, but always 62 steps.
guide.approach:
`diff = a ^ b`. While `diff` is non-zero: `diff &= diff - 1`, `count += 1`.

Dry run 44 ^ 37 = `001001`. `1001 & 1000 = 1000` (count 1). `1000 & 0111 = 0` (count 2). Answer 2.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of differing bits), at most 62 iterations. Space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Comparing the *counts* of ones (5 and 10 both have two ones yet differ in four positions).
guide.follow_up: Same building block as [Hamming Distance](#/problem/hamming-distance) and [Number of 1 Bits](#/problem/number-of-1-bits).

ctci-swap-neighbor-bits.title: Swap Neighbouring Bits
ctci-swap-neighbor-bits.description:
In a 32-bit unsigned number, number the bit positions from 0 (least significant). Swap every even-position bit with the odd-position bit directly above it: bit 0 with bit 1, bit 2 with bit 3, and so on. Return the result.

Use as few operations as you can; a loop over the 16 pairs is not needed.

**Constraints:** `0 <= x < 2^32`.

**Example:** `x = 0b0110_1001` (105) → `0b1001_0110` (150)

guide.prereqs: Masks written in hexadecimal: see [Bits in Python](#/lesson/neet-greedy-math/bits-python).
guide.intuition: Treat all 16 pairs at once. Pick out the odd-position bits with one mask and slide them down; pick out the even-position bits with another mask and slide them up; merge.
hints: What does the hexadecimal digit `A` look like in binary? And `5`?
`0xAAAAAAAA` selects the odd positions, `0x55555555` the even ones.
Shift the odd group right by one, the even group left by one, and OR them.
guide.brute_force: For each of the 16 pairs, read both bits and, if they differ, flip both: 16 iterations instead of 5 operations.
guide.complexity: O(1) time and space.
guide.pitfalls: Swapping the two masks moves bits the wrong way and loses information. Shifting without masking first smears neighbours together.
guide.follow_up: Reverse all 32 bits by repeating the idea with groups of 2, 4, 8 and 16: see [Reverse Bits](#/problem/reverse-bits).

ctci-longest-ones-one-flip.title: Longest Run After One Flip
ctci-longest-ones-one-flip.description:
A 32-bit unsigned number `x` is shown as a row of 32 lamps (1 = on). You may switch **exactly one** lamp from off to on. What is the length of the longest unbroken stretch of lit lamps you can obtain?

If all 32 lamps are already on, the answer is 32.

**Constraints:** `0 <= x < 2^32`. Aim for O(1) extra memory (no list of run lengths).

**Example:** `x = 0b1110110111` (951) → `6` (turn on one of the 0s: it joins a run of three with the run of two)

guide.prereqs: Reading bits one at a time with `x & 1` and `x >>= 1`: see [Bit tricks](#/lesson/neet-greedy-math/bit-tricks).
guide.intuition: Flipping a 0 joins the run of 1s on its right with the run of 1s on its left. Scan the bits once, remembering the length of the current run and the length of the run that came just before the most recent 0.
hints: Write the number as alternating run lengths, e.g. `111 0 1111 0 11`. A flip merges two neighbouring runs of 1s only if a *single* 0 separates them.
Keep `current` (ones since the last 0) and `previous` (the run before that 0, or 0 if that 0 was followed by another 0).
Candidate answer at each step: `previous + 1 + current`.
guide.brute_force: Try each of the 32 positions: set the bit, measure the longest run. 32 × 32 steps; perfectly reasonable to mention as the first idea.
guide.approach:
Scan from the low bit. On a 1: `current += 1`. On a 0: if the next bit is 1 the left run can still be joined, so `previous = current`, else `previous = 0`; then `current = 0`. Track `previous + current + 1`.

Dry run `1110110111` from the right: three 1s (current 3, candidate 4); a 0 followed by a 1 → previous 3, current 0; two 1s → candidate 3+2+1 = 6; next 0 → previous 2; three 1s → 2+3+1 = 6. Best 6.
guide.complexity: Time O(32) = O(1), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Adding 1 to the longest existing run ignores the merge (the wrong solution gives 4 for the example). Returning 33 when every bit is set. Returning 0 for `x = 0` (the answer is 1).
guide.follow_up: The array form is [Max Consecutive Ones III](#/problem/max-consecutive-ones-iii) with k = 1: a sliding window that tolerates one zero.

ctci-next-same-weight.title: Next Number With the Same Weight
ctci-next-same-weight.description:
The **weight** of a positive integer is the number of 1 bits in its binary form. Given `x`, return the **smallest integer greater than `x`** that has the same weight.

**Constraints:** `1 <= x < 2^60`.

**Example 1:** `x = 6 (110)` → `9 (1001)`

**Example 2:** `x = 22 (10110)` → `25 (11001)`

guide.prereqs: Lowest set bit `x & -x` and how addition carries: see [Bit tricks](#/lesson/neet-greedy-math/bit-tricks).
guide.intuition: To get a bigger number you must turn some 0 into a 1; to keep the weight you must turn a 1 into a 0 somewhere *below* it. Choose the lowest 0 that has a 1 to its right (so the increase is as small as possible), flip it, then push all the lower 1s as far right as they can go (so the tail is as small as possible).
hints: Write a few examples in binary: 0110 → 1001, 1011 → 1101, 111000 → 1000011.
Find the rightmost block of 1s. Its top neighbour (a 0) becomes 1; one 1 from the block is used up for that.
The remaining 1s of the block move to the very bottom.
guide.brute_force: Count the weight, then test `x+1`, `x+2`, … until the weight matches. For `x = 2^59` that is about 2^59 tests.
guide.approach:
`lowest = x & -x` isolates the lowest 1. `ripple = x + lowest` clears the rightmost block and sets the 0 above it. `x ^ ripple` is that whole changed region; dividing by `lowest` and shifting right by 2 leaves the block's remaining ones (block length minus one) right-aligned. OR them in.

Dry run `x = 0110`: lowest `0010`, ripple `1000`, `x ^ ripple = 1110`, `>> 2 = 11`, `// 2 = 1`. Result `1001` = 9.
guide.complexity: O(1) arithmetic operations.
guide.pitfalls: Stopping after the ripple (gives 8 for 6, weight 1). Doubling keeps the weight but is rarely the *next* one.
guide.follow_up: Write `prevSameWeight` (mirror image: flip the lowest 1 that has a 0 below it). This is the standard way to enumerate all k-element subsets as bit masks, known as Gosper's hack.

ctci-binary-fraction.title: Binary Fraction Printer
ctci-binary-fraction.description:
A fraction strictly between 0 and 1 is given exactly as `num / den`. Print its binary expansion as a string that starts with `"0."`, for example `5/8 = 0.101` in binary (one half plus one eighth).

If the expansion needs **more than 32 binary digits** after the point (or never ends), return `"ERROR"`.

**Constraints:** `1 <= num < den <= 2^40`.

**Example 1:** `num = 5, den = 8` → `"0.101"`

**Example 2:** `num = 1, den = 3` → `"ERROR"` (0.010101… never terminates)

guide.prereqs: Place value after the binary point (halves, quarters, eighths): see [Bits and bytes](#/lesson/csapp/bits-bytes).
guide.intuition: In decimal, multiplying 0.37 by 10 pushes the first digit (3) in front of the point. Binary works the same with 2: double the fraction; if the result reaches 1 the next digit is 1 (and you subtract 1), otherwise it is 0.
hints: What does doubling do to 0.101 in binary? It becomes 1.01.
Work with the exact pair (num, den) rather than a float: doubling is `num *= 2`, "reached 1" is `num >= den`.
Stop when `num` becomes 0. If you are about to produce a 33rd digit, give up.
guide.brute_force: Subtract 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, … greedily using floating point. It works for short cases but floats themselves have only 53 bits and cannot represent 1/10 exactly, so the output depends on rounding.
guide.approach:
Loop while `num != 0`: if 32 digits already exist return `ERROR`; double; emit 1 and subtract `den` if `num >= den`, else emit 0.

Dry run 5/8: double → 10/8 ≥ 1 → digit 1, left 2/8; double → 4/8 → 0; double → 8/8 → 1, left 0. Result `0.101`.
guide.complexity: At most 32 iterations: O(1) time and space.
guide.pitfalls: Allowing only 31 digits. Rejecting every denominator that is not a power of two: `5/10` is `1/2` and prints fine, so reduce first or let the loop decide.
guide.follow_up: Detect a repeating expansion and print it as `0.0(01)` by remembering which remainders you have seen: see LeetCode's *Fraction to Recurring Decimal*.

ctci-smooth-number-k.title: K-th Number From Chosen Primes
ctci-smooth-number-k.description:
You are given a short list of distinct prime numbers, `primes`. Call a positive integer **buildable** when it can be written as a product that uses only those primes, each as many times as you like (including zero times). The number 1, the empty product, is buildable.

For `primes = [2, 7, 11]` the buildable numbers in increasing order begin `1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 14, 16, 22, 28, …` (6 is missing because it needs the factor 3).

Return the `k`-th buildable number (1-based).

**Constraints:** `1 <= k <= 5000`; between 1 and 6 distinct primes, each below 50, in any order.

**Example 1:** `k = 1, primes = [2, 7, 11]` → `1`

**Example 2:** `k = 9, primes = [2, 7, 11]` → `22`

guide.prereqs: Prime factorisation and merging sorted sequences: see [Number theory](#/lesson/neet-greedy-math/number-theory).
guide.intuition: Every buildable number except 1 is an earlier buildable number multiplied by one of the primes. So the sequence is the merge of several sorted streams, one per prime: (sequence × p). Keep one pointer per stream and always take the smallest head.
hints: With primes 2, 7, 11, how is 14 produced? 7 × 2 or 2 × 7. Notice the same value can come from two streams.
Keep one index into the answer list for each prime.
After choosing the minimum, advance **every** pointer whose head equals it, so duplicates are skipped.
guide.brute_force: Test every integer by dividing out the primes. The buildable numbers thin out so quickly that the 5000-th can be far beyond anything a counting loop reaches. A min-heap with a visited set works in O(k log k).
guide.approach:
`seq = [1]`, `at = [0, 0, 0]`. Heads: `seq[at[j]] * primes[j]`. Append the minimum and advance the matching pointer(s).

Dry run with 2, 7, 11: heads 2, 7, 11 → 2. Heads 4, 7, 11 → 4. Heads 8, 7, 11 → 7. Heads 8, 14, 11 → 8. Heads 14, 14, 11 → 11. Heads 14, 14, 22 → 14, and both the 2-pointer and the 7-pointer advance.
guide.complexity: Time O(k · p) for p primes, space O(k).
guide.pitfalls: Advancing only the first pointer that matches leaves a duplicate in the list (14 would appear twice; first wrong solution). Accepting every multiple of a listed prime (second wrong solution) lets in numbers such as 6, which also needs the factor 3.
guide.follow_up: With the fixed primes 2, 3, 5 this is [Ugly Number II](#/problem/ugly-number-ii). With many primes, replace the scan for the minimum by a heap: LeetCode's *Super Ugly Number*.

ctci-dice-sum-probability.title: Chance of a Dice Total
ctci-dice-sum-probability.description:
You roll `n` fair six-sided dice. What is the probability that the faces add up to exactly `total`?

Return the exact answer as a fraction in lowest terms, `[numerator, denominator]`. Return `[0, 1]` when the total is impossible.

**Constraints:** `1 <= n <= 30`; `0 <= total <= 200`.

**Example 1:** `n = 2, total = 7` → `[1, 6]` (6 of the 36 outcomes)

**Example 2:** `n = 1, total = 9` → `[0, 1]`

guide.prereqs: Probability as favourable outcomes divided by all outcomes, and counting with dynamic programming: see [DP for counting](#/lesson/neet-dp/dp-counting-states).
guide.intuition: All `6^n` sequences of faces are equally likely, so the probability is (number of sequences with the right sum) / `6^n`. Count the sequences one die at a time: the ways to reach sum `s` with `d` dice come from the ways to reach `s-1 … s-6` with `d-1` dice.
hints: The totals are not equally likely (there are 11 possible totals for two dice but 7 has probability 1/6).
Let `ways[s]` = number of ordered rolls of the dice so far that add to `s`. Start with zero dice: `ways[0] = 1`.
After the table is filled, reduce `ways[total] / 6^n` with `math.gcd`.
guide.brute_force: Enumerate all `6^n` outcomes with recursion: fine for n ≤ 8, hopeless for n = 30 (about 2·10²³ outcomes).
guide.approach:
Repeat n times: build `nxt` from `ways` by adding each face 1…6. Then reduce the fraction.

Dry run n = 2: after one die `ways[1..6] = 1`. After two dice `ways[7] = ways[1]+…+ways[6] = 6`. Fraction 6/36 → `[1, 6]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n · total · 6), space O(total). Python's big integers keep the count exact.
guide.pitfalls: Assuming every total from n to 6n is equally likely. Returning an unreduced fraction. Using floats: 6³⁰ exceeds the 53 bits a float holds exactly.
guide.follow_up: The counting core is LeetCode's *Number of Dice Rolls With Target Sum*. Try answering "at least `total`" with a suffix sum.

ctci-lamp-toggle.title: Pier Lamps
ctci-lamp-toggle.description:
A long pier is lit by `n` lamps numbered `1 … n`, all switched off at dusk. During the night a maintenance routine makes `n` passes along the pier: on pass `k` it presses the switch of every lamp whose number is a multiple of `k`, and each press flips that lamp (off ↔ on).

When the last pass is over, how many lamps are on?

**Constraints:** `0 <= n <= 10^18`. A simulation is far too slow; find the pattern.

**Example 1:** `n = 10` → `3` (lamps 1, 4 and 9)

**Example 2:** `n = 3` → `1`

guide.prereqs: Divisors of a number: see [Number theory](#/lesson/neet-greedy-math/number-theory).
guide.intuition: Lamp `L` is flipped once for every divisor of `L`. It ends on when it is flipped an odd number of times. Divisors come in pairs (`d` and `L/d`), so the count is even unless some divisor is paired with itself, which happens exactly when `L` is a perfect square.
hints: Simulate n = 10 by hand and write down which lamps end on.
How many times is lamp 12 flipped? List its divisors and pair them up.
Count the perfect squares up to `n`: that is the integer square root of `n`.
guide.brute_force: Simulate with an array: pass k flips n/k lamps, total about n ln n operations. Fine for n = 10⁵, impossible for 10¹⁸.
guide.approach:
Return `math.isqrt(n)`.

Dry run n = 10: squares ≤ 10 are 1, 4, 9 → 3. Lamp 4 has divisors 1, 2, 4 (three flips: on, off, on).
guide.complexity: O(1) arithmetic (isqrt is O(log n) bit operations).
guide.pitfalls: `int(n ** 0.5)` uses floating point and is off by one for large `n`: for `n = 10^18 - 1` the float square root rounds up to exactly 10⁹. Use `math.isqrt`.
guide.follow_up: Follow-ups: which lamps are flipped exactly twice (the primes)? Which are flipped exactly three times (squares of primes)? The same divisor-pairing argument appears in LeetCode's *Bulb Switcher* and in the lockers puzzle of the lesson.

ctci-two-phone-drop.title: Two Phones, One Tower
ctci-two-phone-drop.description:
